# Environmental change. Economic systems. Equitable development.

**360 Political Ecology (360PE)** examines how environmental change, economic systems, political institutions, resource governance and social equity shape sustainable development.

Through **360PE Review**, we connect credible research with interdisciplinary interpretation, political-ecological analysis and informed policy dialogue.

**Evidence · Ecology · Equity · Development**

[Read 360PE Review](publications.qmd){.pe-button}
:::

## Why 360PE exists

Environmental and development challenges are interconnected. Climate change, energy transitions, natural resource extraction, ecological degradation and economic inequality cannot be adequately understood through a single disciplinary perspective.

360PE brings economic, ecological, political and social perspectives together to examine these challenges, communicate research evidence and explore their implications for more equitable and sustainable development.

::: {.pe-home-grid}
::: {.pe-home-card}
### Our mission

To generate, synthesize and share credible, evidence-informed knowledge that contributes to fairer, more sustainable and more resilient societies.
:::
::: {.pe-home-card}
### Our purpose

To make complex environmental and development questions understandable, relevant and actionable for researchers, policymakers, practitioners, students and the wider public—without sacrificing scientific rigor, contextual understanding or appropriate recognition of uncertainty.
:::
:::

## How we work: from evidence to policy understanding

360PE Review applies a **five-stage Evidence-to-Policy Framework** to connect empirical findings with critical interpretation and wider development implications.

The framework guides research communication and policy analysis. It does not presume that every publication establishes causal relationships or demonstrates the effectiveness of proposed interventions.

<div class="pe-work-grid" role="list" aria-label="360PE five-stage evidence-to-policy framework">
  <div class="pe-work-step" role="listitem">
    <span>01</span>
    <strong>Finding</strong>
    <p>Present documented observations, research results and credible quantitative evidence.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="pe-work-step" role="listitem">
    <span>02</span>
    <strong>Explanation</strong>
    <p>Clarify meanings, definitions, context, methods, limitations and uncertainties.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="pe-work-step" role="listitem">
    <span>03</span>
    <strong>Expert interpretation</strong>
    <p>Engage attributable expert knowledge, relevant scholarship and alternative explanations.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="pe-work-step" role="listitem">
    <span>04</span>
    <strong>Political-ecological analysis</strong>
    <p>Examine economic incentives, institutions, power relationships, ecological processes and distributional consequences.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="pe-work-step" role="listitem">
    <span>05</span>
    <strong>Development and policy implications</strong>
    <p>Consider governance responses, implementation constraints, trade-offs and potential development outcomes.</p>
  </div>
</div>

**Our editorial approach:** Present the evidence. Explain its meaning. Engage expert knowledge. Examine the political-economic and ecological mechanisms. Connect the findings to wider development and policy implications.

[Learn more about our analytical approach →](about.qmd#our-five-stage-evidence-to-policy-framework)

## Featured research

::: {.pe-callout}
**360PE Review | Issue 01**

### [Africa's Battery Minerals: Can Export Bans Deliver Sustainable Industrialization?](articles/africa-battery-minerals/index.qmd)

A comparative policy synthesis examining whether mineral export restrictions can support sustainable industrialization in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zimbabwe and Indonesia.

The analysis considers productive capabilities, public value capture, resource governance, ecological integrity, institutional constraints and the distribution of development benefits.

It distinguishes observed policy outcomes from proposed causal mechanisms and identifies questions requiring further empirical evaluation.

[Read the complete article →](articles/africa-battery-minerals/index.qmd)
:::

## What we study

360PE Review organizes its research and analysis around **ten interconnected thematic areas**, encompassing environmental change, economic development, political ecology, sustainability and international environmental governance.

Our homepage presents these areas in three broad groupings for accessibility. The [Topics page](topics.qmd) provides the official thematic categories.

::: {.pe-tiles}
::: {.pe-tile}
**Climate, energy and industrial transitions**

Climate change and resilience; energy and resource economics; critical minerals, industrial development and energy transitions.
:::
::: {.pe-tile}
**Justice, governance and ecosystems**

Environmental justice and health; environmental governance and political ecology; biodiversity, ecosystems and ecological sustainability.
:::
::: {.pe-tile}
**Development, finance and international policy**

Sustainable development; climate and sustainable finance; just transition; international environmental policy and law.
:::
:::

[Explore all ten official research areas →](topics.qmd)

## What guides our analysis

360PE's editorial and analytical work is organized around four guiding principles.

::: {.pe-home-grid}
::: {.pe-home-card}
### Evidence

Prioritize credible sources, transparent attribution, methodological clarity and responsible interpretation of research findings.
:::
::: {.pe-home-card}
### Ecology

Examine environmental systems, ecological relationships, resource use and the consequences of environmental change.
:::
::: {.pe-home-card}
### Equity

Consider environmental justice, participation, distributional consequences and the allocation of development benefits and costs.
:::
::: {.pe-home-card}
### Development

Connect environmental and economic analysis with institutional capacity, policy choices, sustainability and long-term societal well-being.
:::
:::

These principles guide the questions we ask and the evidence we examine. They do not predetermine our empirical conclusions.

## Our guiding question

> What does the evidence show, who benefits, who bears the costs, and how can development become more just and sustainable?

360PE approaches environmental challenges as interconnected scientific, economic, institutional, ecological and distributive questions.

## Join the conversation

360PE welcomes informed critique, research collaborations, interdisciplinary dialogue and constructive contributions from researchers, policymakers, practitioners, students and the wider public.

**360 Political Ecology was founded by Amanfo Smart Edward, PhD**, an interdisciplinary researcher working across environmental and development economics, sustainability and related policy fields.

360PE operates as an **independent, research-informed publication and analytical platform**. Institutional affiliations mentioned in founder or contributor profiles are provided for identification and do not imply institutional sponsorship, endorsement or editorial responsibility.

**360PE Review is not presented as a peer-reviewed academic journal.** Its publications aim to uphold evidence traceability, accurate attribution, analytical transparency and responsible policy interpretation.
